title: How to spot a romance scammer
summary: How to spot a romance scammer: the signs in their messages, and the checks on their photos, details and investment site. Sixtyfour researches the details.
body_markdown:
Look for the sequence: affection that arrives very fast, a reason they can never meet, a push to move the chat off the app, and then a request for money or an offer to help you invest. Then check what they told you: reverse search their photos, test their name and job story, look up their phone number and email address, and find out whether any investment site is a real company. The FBI's advice is not to invest on the advice of someone you have met only online.


They message constantly, seem to share all your interests and plans, and quickly ask to move to WhatsApp, Telegram or text. Their job or situation keeps them far away, often military service overseas or work offshore. Then comes a crisis that needs money, a request to use your bank account, or talk of their trading success and an offer to teach you.


It is the scammers' own name for cryptocurrency investment fraud that starts with a friendship or romance. The scammer builds trust, coaches the victim onto a fake trading website or app that shows growing profits, and charges taxes or fees when the victim tries to withdraw, and the FBI says victims cannot get their money back even if they pay. INTERPOL has asked for the term romance baiting instead, because the old name shames victims.


Find the platform yourself rather than through a link someone sent you, compare its address letter by letter with any real exchange it resembles, and check the domain's creation date in ICANN's Lookup tool. Look up the company it names in the business registry where it says it is incorporated, and search its name with the words scam and complaint. A platform that shows big profits but asks you to pay a fee or tax before you can withdraw matches the pattern the FBI describes.


Yes. Sixtyfour is a research agent that takes the name, phone number, email address, usernames and employer someone gave you, and the name and website of any investment platform they sent you to, and returns who each detail leads to and what it found about the company, with the sources for each researched field and, when you turn it on, a confidence score. It does not run reverse image searches or see a dating app's own records, and a field it could not establish comes back empty for a person to judge.


Stop sending money, and do not pay any fee or tax to withdraw funds from an investment platform. Contact your bank or the payment company right away, tell them you paid a scammer and ask them to refund your money, then report it to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center, the FTC and the app where you met. Be wary of anyone who offers to recover the money for a fee, because the FBI says those services are often scams too.


They compare the details that reports have in common: the same photos under different names, the same phone number or email address, the same investment website or wallet address, and accounts created close together. Each shared detail is weighed by how many unrelated people could share it, beside the platform's own records. Sixtyfour researches where each identifier leads outside the platform, and Lattice connects reported accounts whose rows share an email address, phone number, profile URL or domain.
